newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW - Argentine utility mulls output hike.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Argentine utility mulls output hike.

text.p: Argentina's Central Costanera -- currently expanding capacity to 2,282 megawatts (MW) by 1998 -- is considering boosting capacity by an additional 25 percent to meet growing demand, a top official said Monday.

"We are mulling projects to increase capacity by about 25 percent once the new 832.5 MW plant we ordered is commercially operative by December 1998," General Manager Miguel Ortiz Fuentes told Reuters in an interview.
But he declined to give more details on any contemplated projects and the required investment.
Central Costanera last year awarded a $280 million turnkey contract to Japan's Mitsubishi Corp for the building of a combined cycle 832.5 MW plant.
The plant will raise Central Costanera's gross capacity to 2,282 MW from current 1,450 MW, including 320 MW from its Central Trmoelctrica Buenos Aires.

Central Costanera, one of the country's two biggest thermoelectric generating companies, has a nine percent share in the Argentine market and plans to have about 12 percent once the new plant becomes operational. Central Puerto, run by Chile's Chilgener SA, has 13 percent of the market.
The controlling 51 percent stake in Central Costanera is owned by Chile's ENDESA, which in turn is controlled by Chile's ENERSIS SA.
Ortiz Fuentes said the company forsees Argentine electricity demand doubling over the next decade, at a rate of seven percent annual growth.
"There is a lot of room to grow," he said, noting Argentine electricity consumption was relatively low at 1,650 KW/hour per capita per year.
By comparision, U.S. per capita consumption was between 11,000 to 12,000 KW/hour, he said.
Ortiz Fuentes said that for 1997 the company expects electricity-related revenue similar to fiscal 1996's $313 million.
Last year the company posted a $48 million net profit.
Central Costanera is interested in the privatization, expected later this year, of Buenos Aires province utility ESEBA, valued by the government at $1 billion.
But Ortiz Fuentes the firm was just interested in the generating sector of ESEBA, which will be divided for sale in generation, distribution and transport facilities.
He said ESEBA's sale was tied to complicated deals involving the payment for gas, even if it is not used.
Ortiz Fuentes said the company forecast a decline in electricity prices to about $22 from current $23 towards the end of the century due to a booming supply.
Prices were then seen to stabilize on the back of an expected increase in consumption.
Ortiz Fuentes said the company was interested in selling energy to Brazil, which this month announced that it would buy initially about 1,000 MW of electricity from Argentina.
